newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Britain attacked for handling of BSE crisis.
newsitem.headline: Britain attacked for handling of BSE crisis.

text.p: Britain stopped European Union inspectors checking in the early 1990s if measures to fight mad cow disease were being implemented, the head of a European Parliament inquiry said on Wednesday.

Reimer Boege, the German Christian Democrat president of the inquiry, said Britain's chief Veterinary Officer Keith Meldrum had said in June 1990 that there was no legal authority for an EU inspection.
"Meldrum...said the EU inspectors had no mandate to inspect BSE measures," Boege told a news conference.
It was unacceptable that the EU had failed to make any inspections in Britain into the disease, known scientificially as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), between 1990 and 1994, he said.
"It is quite clear to most (committee) members that the fight against BSE was not organised as might have been expected," Boege said.

Since September, the special parliamentary committee has been investigating alleged mishandling of the crisis, which erupted in March after Britain created consumer panic by disclosing that the fatal cattle brain disease could spread to people.
A report on Tuesday predicted that hundreds of Britons would die annually from eating beef infected with the BSE.

Boege, a former dairy farmer, said that EU member states --, notably Britain where the epidemic is concentrated -- and the EU's executive Commission must share responsibility for failing to implement EU animal feed and other anti-BSE measures.
"There was an enormous lack of control and loss of public confidence," he said.

Britain had argued against the EU inspections saying BSE was a political, not a technical matter, but Boege said that British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg had twice refused invitations to come before the committee.
Instead Hogg sent the senior official in the Ministry of Agriculture, Richard Packer, who argued that the BSE crisis was an "act of God" and that the British government was only 30 percent to blame.
"If there have been faults in administration and organisation...it is the political responsibility of ministers," Boege said.
In January 1991, Meldrum told a Christian Democrat parliamentary hearing that 20,000 cattle were affected by BSE and that everything was under control.
Around 165,000 British cattle have now been struck down by the disease since the first case was reported in 1986. Fewer than 600 cases have been reported in other European countries.
Meldrum, along with EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler, is due to appear before the committee on December 3.

The parliament will not vote on the committee's report until February 6, 1997, but its author issued provisional conclusions early last month urging the European Commission to ask the European Court of Justice to make Britain compensate its EU partners for losses caused by the crisis.
